newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco begins court fights over Liggett papers.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco begins court fights over Liggett papers.

text.p: The tobacco industry on Monday stepped up its offensive aimed at stopping Liggett Group from releasing potentially damaging documents by asking judges in several states to block their dissemination.

Hearings were held in at least three states, Illinois, Texas and Arizona, following Liggett's historic agreement last Thursday to turn over over internal documents as part of a settlement with 22 state attorneys general who have sued the major cigarette makers to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers.

Under the accord, the documents will be given to judges presiding over the 22 suits. The judges will determine whether the documents can be used as evidence or if they are protected by attorney-client privilege.

The tobacco industry had quickly obtained a restraining order last Thursday from a North Carolina state court preventing Liggett, which is owned by Bennett LeBow's Brooke Group, Inc., from handing over documents that might reveal joint legal defence efforts by the cigarette companies.
The manufacturers are now in the process of asking various courts to honour that injunction.

A source close to settlement talks told Reuters that boxes of documents have already been shipped to several states, including Mississippi, Florida and Texas, where trials are scheduled to begin this year.

Some documents have also been sent to the Department of Justice, which is conducting a criminal investigation into whether the industry withheld information from government agencies about health risks of smoking, government sources told Reuters.
The industry argues that the documents must be kept secret because they are the result of confidential communications between lawyers and their clients.

However, attorneys general have played down the importance of the injunction. During a news conference last week to announce the settlement, they said the injunction was not binding on courts in other states.
They also said the documents would not be protected if they are found to contain evidence of crime or fraud.
Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, who is spear-heading the Medicaid litigation, said he was confident the North Carolina injunction would not stop the release of the documents.
"That dog won't hunt," he told the news conference. The Mississippi trial is the first scheduled to proceed on June 2.
In Florida, attorneys involved in the state's Medicaid suit said Monday they want court-appointed special master William Rutter to review the Liggett documents in private.

Rutter has reviewed scores of other internal industry documents for the trial judge, Palm Beach County Circuit Court Judge Harold Cohen, and would recommend to Cohen whether all Liggett documents, none of them, or only some of them should be used at trial.
Lawyers said the Liggett documents would be discussed at a hearing before Rutter on Wednesday morning in West Palm Beach, Florida.
Florida's suit is scheduled for trial beginning Aug. 4.
Last Friday Dade County Judge Alan Postman said during a pre-trial hearing in a separate, class-action suit against tobacco companies that he wanted to see the Liggett documents as soon as possible.
